name: Mathnasium
line: Mathnasium teaches in scheduled sessions, in a center or online. AMP gives checked, explained practice any day.
description: AMP vs Mathnasium: live instructors in scheduled sessions against checked, adaptive math practice at home on any day. Price, method, review and evidence.
verdict: Mathnasium puts a live instructor with a child, in a center or online, and for a child who needs a person, that is a real strength [1][7]. It recommends two to three sessions a week and assigns no homework, its FAQ sends families to a local center for prices, and its results page gives percentages with no stated method [1][3]. AMP brings checked, explained practice home on any day, brings each old skill back on a schedule, and puts its price on its website.

reasons.title: Math happens between center visits too
reasons.body: Mathnasium recommends two to three sessions a week and assigns no homework; part of each session goes to the child's school homework [1]. AMP is open at home on any day. Every answer is checked at once and followed by the correct answer and worked steps, and unlimited workbooks made for the learner print with a worked answer key. Across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, feedback that explains did best [11].

reasons.title: AMP's price is on its website
reasons.body: Mathnasium lists no prices. Its FAQ describes a flat enrollment fee with regular attendance, says pricing varies by program and area, and sends families to a local center; it also says it typically costs less than private tutoring [1]. AMP costs $599 a year or $59 a month for the first child, and $399 or $39 for each child after. That pays for placement, every problem chosen and checked, scheduled review and unlimited workbooks, from counting through precalculus. The first 100 answers and 5 workbooks are free, with no card.

reasons.title: The plan changes at every answer
reasons.body: Mathnasium builds a customized learning plan from a written and verbal assessment [1][2]. One center explains that each missed question becomes a skill in the plan, that a Progress Check partway through can move a student along, and that a new plan follows a new assessment [6]. AMP keeps a level in each of 14 strands of math and updates it after every answer given without help. From that it picks each next problem: new work, a prerequisite, or review. Two misses in a row on a skill send practice back to what that skill builds on.

reasons.title: Each old skill comes back on a schedule
reasons.body: One Mathnasium center describes how it checks retention: a Progress Check about halfway through a learning plan, a Post-Assessment at its end, and skills not yet mastered folded into the next plan [6]. AMP brings each learned skill back on its own schedule, after 6 hours, 1 day, 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks and a month, mixed with other topics, and a miss restarts the schedule. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [10].

reasons.title: Every rule is public
reasons.body: Mathnasium describes its curriculum as proprietary [4]. One center describes its mastery check: after 10 to 20 pages on a skill, the student does a page without the instructor's help [6]. AMP's code is open source, so anyone can read its mastery rule (four of the last five right without help), its review schedule and its grading. An answer given after a hint or the lesson never counts toward mastery.

rows.price: Not listed. The FAQ says pricing varies by program and area and sends families to a local center. It says it typically costs less than private tutoring [1].
rows.buyers: Families, through a local center. Enrollment starts with a form and a free assessment [4].
rows.range: Kindergarten through grade 12 [1]. Levels of number sense, then algebra readiness, then algebra and higher math [2].
rows.start: A free written and verbal assessment at enrollment, which can cover topics school has not reached yet [1][4].
rows.teaching: A live instructor, in a center or online [7], working through talk, pictures, writing, mental math and physical objects [2].
rows.next: A customized learning plan built from the assessment [1][2]. One center turns each missed question into a skill and works on three skills at a time [6].
rows.mastery: A mastery check after 10 to 20 pages on a skill, done without the instructor's help, as one center describes it [6].
rows.review: Retention checked at milestones, in one center's account: a Progress Check about halfway through a learning plan and a Post-Assessment at its end [6].
rows.print: Work is done in the center; one center says its pages are on iPads [6]. No homework is sent home [1].
rows.adult: Little: an instructor teaches each session, and no homework is assigned [1].
rows.reports: One center sends parents a monthly progress report (attendance, skills mastered and remaining) and makes a monthly call [6].
rows.evidence: Results-page percentages with no sample or method [3]. An FAQ claim of independent studies, none named [1]. No Evidence for ESSA entry and no WWC intervention report [8][9].

theirs: Mathnasium is a chain of after-school math learning centers. It was founded in Los Angeles in 2002, began franchising in 2003, and most centers are franchises [5]. Its FAQ counts more than 1,000 centers in the U.S. [1], and it also offers live online tutoring, Mathnasium@home [7]. It serves kindergarten through grade 12 and describes itself as an after-school mathematics program [1][4].

A family starts by contacting a local center and booking a free assessment, written and verbal [1][4]. From it the center builds a customized learning plan [2]. An instructor teaches for understanding, starting from what the child already knows, with mental, visual, verbal, hands-on and written work [2]. It recommends two to three sessions a week; part of each session goes to the child's school homework, and no homework is assigned [1].

The method is built around number sense: counting, wholes and parts, proportional thinking and related themes, across seven levels, then algebra readiness and higher math [2]. One center describes the cycle: three skills at a time, 10 to 20 pages on each, then a mastery check done without the instructor's help; a Progress Check partway through the plan; and a Post-Assessment at the end, where 85% marks a level as mastered [6].
credit: A live instructor teaches face to face, with talk, pictures, writing and physical objects [2]. AMP has no live teacher, and its few built models are on screen.
A person places the child: a free written and verbal assessment at enrollment that can reach past what school has taught [1][4].
Help with current school homework is part of each session [1]. AMP practices its own problems.
More than 1,000 centers in the U.S. [1], plus live online sessions with its instructors through Mathnasium@home [7]. Someone else runs math time, with no homework to oversee [1].

theirs: Mathnasium's results page, under the heading "Proven Outcomes", gives three numbers: 94% of parents report improved skills and understanding, 93% report an improved attitude, and 90% of students saw improved school grades [3]. The page gives no sample size, method, date or comparison group. Two of the numbers are labeled as parent reports, and none is presented as a measured result.

Its FAQ says the method has been "proven through the success of hundreds of thousands of students" [1]. A count of past students is not a comparison with students who did not attend. The FAQ also says multiple independent studies found better scores on standards-based tests in 20 sessions or fewer, but it names no study and gives no sample or result [1]. As of November 2026 it has no entry in Evidence for ESSA and no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report [8][9].

Tutoring as a whole has strong evidence. Across 263 randomized trials the average effect was 0.40 standard deviations, and 0.16 to 0.22 for large U.S. programs measured on standardized tests [12]. Those are averages across many tutoring programs, not results for Mathnasium.
ours: AMP's rules come from findings that bear on the days between center visits. Feedback that explains averaged 0.49 across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, against 0.05 for marking right or wrong alone [11]. Mixed, spaced practice scored 62% against 38% a month later, in a randomized trial that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations [10]. We think checked, explained practice most days, with old skills returning on a schedule, gives a learner something center time alone does not. That is our bet, and we have committed to testing it in public.

AMP is new, and its own outcome studies have not run yet. They begin in 2027: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. Until then, the research behind each part of AMP is laid out in our report, and the code is public.

them: Your child needs a person in the room to explain, notice frustration and encourage.
Your child learns best by talking math through and handling real objects.
You want help with this week's school homework as part of each session.
There is a center nearby and you want math handled outside the home, with no homework.
amp: You want math most days at home, not only on center days.
You want to see the price and try it free before you commit.
You want every miss explained and old skills brought back on a schedule, without planning it.
Your child already goes to Mathnasium and you want checked practice between visits.
Your learner is far ahead or behind in one part of math and needs each strand placed on its own.

questions.question: How much does Mathnasium cost?
questions.answer: Mathnasium does not list prices. Its FAQ says pricing varies by program and area and sends families to a local center [1]. It says it typically costs less than private tutoring [1]. AMP is $599 a year or $59 a month for the first child, and the first 100 answers are free.

questions.question: Does Mathnasium give homework?
questions.answer: No. Mathnasium assigns no homework and sets aside session time for school homework [1]. AMP prints unlimited workbooks made for each learner, with worked answer keys, and results entered from paper count toward the learner's level.

questions.question: Is Mathnasium proven to work?
questions.answer: Its results page reports percentages with no sample or method [3]. Its FAQ cites independent studies but names none [1]. It has no entry in Evidence for ESSA and no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report [8][9].

questions.question: Can my child use AMP and Mathnasium at the same time?
questions.answer: Yes. AMP is a separate web program that places the learner within the first 24 problems and keeps a level in each of 14 strands. Mathnasium assigns no homework [1], so practice on AMP at home does not compete with center homework.

questions.question: Does AMP replace a tutor?
questions.answer: No. AMP has no live teacher. It gives practice at the learner's level, with a hint, a lesson and worked steps for every problem, and it can sit beside a tutor or a center.
